subject: biology

moments.title: Bernal and Crowfoot — first protein crystal X-ray pattern
moments.who: J. D. Bernal and Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin, Cambridge
moments.body:
Bernal and his student Dorothy Crowfoot obtain the first X-ray diffraction pattern of a protein crystal (pepsin). It shows that proteins have defined three-dimensional structures with regular features.

Crowfoot Hodgkin will go on to solve penicillin (1945), vitamin B12 (1956), and insulin (1969), winning the 1964 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
moments.takeaway: Proteins are not amorphous. They have defined structures, which X-ray crystallography can in principle reveal.

moments.title: Pauling proposes the alpha helix
moments.who: Linus Pauling and Robert Corey, Caltech
moments.body:
Pauling and Corey work out the geometry of polypeptide chains, allowing for hydrogen bonding. They predict that proteins should commonly contain an alpha helix and a beta sheet. They build the helix using paper models, in bed while Pauling has flu.

They publish before any X-ray data confirms it. Within months, model and data match.
moments.takeaway: Theoretical chemistry predicts protein structural motifs from first principles. Experimentation confirms.

moments.title: Kendrew solves myoglobin
moments.body:
John Kendrew, working at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, solves the structure of sperm whale myoglobin — the oxygen-storage protein of muscle. The first three-dimensional protein structure.

The structure looks ugly: an asymmetric tangle with no obvious symmetry. Pauling had hoped for elegance; he gets a 'visceral lump'. But it's REAL.

quote.text: Perhaps the most striking features of the molecule are its complexity and its lack of symmetry. The arrangement seems to be almost totally lacking in the kind of regularities which one instinctively anticipates.

moments.takeaway: The first protein structure is irregular. Functional sophistication arises from specific, asymmetric folds — not from neat geometry.

moments.title: Perutz solves hemoglobin
moments.body:
Max Perutz, after 22 years of work, solves the structure of hemoglobin. He shares the 1962 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Kendrew.

Hemoglobin is four similar subunits, each like myoglobin. Perutz later works out the structural changes during oxygen binding — the molecular basis of cooperative binding (T state vs R state).
moments.takeaway: Multi-subunit proteins are now structurally accessible. Conformational changes drive function.

moments.title: AlphaFold
moments.body:
DeepMind's AlphaFold 2 predicts protein structures from sequence with accuracy comparable to experimental methods. The 'protein folding problem' — predicting structure from sequence — had been considered one of biology's biggest unsolved problems.

The AlphaFold database (2022) contains predicted structures for ~200 million proteins — essentially all known proteins. The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry goes to John Jumper, Demis Hassabis (AlphaFold) and David Baker (de novo protein design).
moments.takeaway: An AI system effectively solves a 50-year-old central problem of biochemistry. Most known proteins now have a predicted structure.

now.title: Protein structure today
now.body:
We have experimental structures for ~200,000 proteins and predicted structures for ~200 million. Cryo-EM (single-particle) is now solving structures at near-atomic resolution without crystallisation. AlphaFold and related tools predict effects of mutations, ligand binding, design new proteins.

Applications: structure-based drug design (almost all modern drug discovery), enzyme engineering, vaccine design, understanding genetic disease.
now.open_questions: How do proteins fold dynamically (the kinetic, not just final, problem)? Can we design proteins with novel functions reliably? How do disordered proteins work? What happens when proteins misfold (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's)?

reflection: Kendrew's first structure was ugly. Many later structures are not 'beautiful' by Pauling's standard either. Beauty in biology emerges at a higher level — the function works, not because the shape is symmetric, but because asymmetric details position atoms exactly where chemistry needs them. How often is our aesthetic intuition a poor guide to scientific reality?
